transcript:
<Meeting Header>
Date: 2026-09-14
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Ava Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Meridian Labs - Head of ML), Ethan Cole (Meridian - Platform), Samir Gupta (Meridian - CTO)
Recording ID: ff-20260914-meridian-001

Summary:
- SE-led deep dive on strategies to serve 128k+ context with low tail latency. Discussed hybrid KV sharding across host and dedicated, progressive chunking strategies, attention window optimizations, quantization impacts on cache hit rates, and networking/VPC implications for on-prem vs hosted.

Topics:
- 128k+ prefix handling and chunking heuristics
- KV cache sharding & eviction (LRU vs generational)
- Batching strategies for streaming vs batching latency
- Quantization tradeoffs (8-bit/4-bit mixed)
- VPC/on-prem network topology and NFS/PMEM considerations

[00:00] Ava: all right everyone thanks for joining, uh let's kick off, quick intros
[00:07] Priya: hi this is priya we run inference infra at meridian, our main goal is to get 128k docs searchable in a single session without 2s+ tail latencies
[00:15] Diego: cool, and i'm diego from redwood runtime team — mainly gonna walk through patterns and run some numbers
[00:21] Ethan: quick note we have a hybrid setup right now, some models in cloud, some on prem for pii redaction
[00:27] Samir: and timeline is 8-12 weeks for a pilot if performance looks good

[00:35] Diego: ok first, the basic problem — naive 128k attention is impossible memory wise, so we use chunking + global KV. our question is where to store the KV: in-host GPU ram, remote shard, or a hybrid approach
[00:51] Priya: by K-V you mean the key/value cache from past tokens right? i think our team calls it the K V cash, haha
[00:57] Ava: yeah, k-v cache, it's the KV for attention retrieval — keeps past chunk representations so we don't reencode everything

[01:10] Diego: recommended pattern is progressive chunking: small overlapping chunks (8–16k tokens) converted to compressed KV entries. For extremely long context (128k+) we do a two-level index: short-term local KV for hot prefixes (residing on GPU), and cold KV shards stored on dedicated host or NVMe-backed PMEM with async fetch
[01:32] Ethan: what's the cost of the async fetch on tail latency? if we miss local cache do we add 150-300ms
[01:40] Diego: depends. fetch from co-located host with RDMA could be 20–60ms; NVMe+CPU path more like 80–250ms. but we can mask much of that with speculative prefetching based on recent token ngrams

[02:00] Priya: can you say more about prefetch heuristics? our access patterns are spiky when users navigate docs
[02:07] Diego: sure, heuristic 1: sliding-window frequency — if a chunk is referenced >N times in last M tokens, mark as hot. heuristic 2: conversational affinity — chunks referenced within same convo cluster get priority. heuristic 3: soft TTL for generated sequences
[02:25] Samir: are these heuristics built-in or configurable? we need RBAC so product teams can tweak
[02:30] Ava: configurable via optimize profiles — you can tune thresholds per model and route

[02:40] Diego: eviction policy comparison: pure LRU is simple but suffers thrashing in pattern-shift workloads. we recommend a generational+LFU hybrid: keep tiny GPU resident generation for hottest 5–10% based on recency+frequency, second generation in host RAM, cold in NVMe. Eviction moves entries between tiers rather than dropping immediately
[03:00] Priya: that sounds promising. how big is an entry for a 16k token chunk — like how many bytes
[03:07] Diego: uncompressed float16 kv entry for 16k chunk ~ 256MB for keys+values depending on hidden dim. With quantized 8-bit or 4-bit compressed formats we drop to 60–90MB or 35–50MB respectively
[03:20] Ethan: that's huge — so quantization is key

[03:30] Diego: yes but quantization impacts similarity retrieval quality. we observed recall drop of ~1–3% with 8-bit and 3–8% with 4-bit depending on projection and tokenizer mismatch. For reranking-sensitive apps, you may want higher precision on the last-layer projections
[03:50] Priya: can we do mixed precision — say keep keys in 8-bit and values in 4-bit or fp16 for recent entries?
[03:59] Diego: absolutely. mixed quant scheme often gives sweet spot: keys at 8-bit for nearest-neighbor stability, values at 4-bit for storage, and recent entries pinned in fp16

[04:10] Ava: question from sales angle — customers worry about cost and complexity of Dedicated vs Hosted. can we articulate tradeoffs for meridian's usage
[04:17] Diego: Dedicated gives predictable latency and co-located KV in GPU host — removes network fetchs. Hosted with hybrid storage can be cheaper but needs smarter eviction/prefetch and may see occasional tail spikes. For their 128k use-case, a small Dedicated pool (4-8x A100 equiv) with hybrid KV will give best tail

[04:40] Priya: network/topology — if we run private in our DC, what are the recommendations: SR-IOV, RDMA, NVMe over Fabrics?
[04:49] Diego: RDMA is ideal. NVMe-oF with local CPU proxies works but adds CPU overhead. For PMEM-backed cold shards, prioritize fabrics with <100us for RDMA, <1ms with NVMe-oF. Avoid NAT gateways between GPU hosts and KV store

[05:05] Samir: for on-prem, we have existing Ceph cluster, any red flags?
[05:10] Diego: Ceph is okay for cold storage but avoid synchronous reads for hot paths. We'll deploy a caching layer — a small in-memory host service per rack with direct PCIe NVMe for the hot shard

[05:28] Ethan: batching — what's your recommendation for batches when streaming to client? we need low latency for interactive but throughput for bulk
[05:35] Diego: continuous batching with dynamic cutoffs. For interactive, keep micro-batch latency target <30ms per request; for high throughput async, batch to fill GPU. Redwood runtime does adaptive batching, balancing latency SLOs and token throughput
[05:50] Priya: how do you handle streaming across long context — do you stream partial attention or stream on final output
[05:56] Lina Zhou: (chiming in) we stream tokens as they complete. KV fetches happen in background; if a fetch is pending we can emit partial tokens using local context and auto-correct with edit tokens later — it's a speculative streaming approach

[06:15] Priya: what about correctness? speculative tokens might hallucinate then be corrected — user experience concerns
[06:22] Diego: valid concern. we only speculative when probability mass is stable; and UI should show 'tentative' state. for enterprise doc legal workflows we often disable speculation

[06:35] Ethan: benchmarks — walk us through what you can run to validate latency
[06:40] Diego: we'll run three passes: 1) in-memory best-case with all KV resident, 2) hybrid with host-sharded cold fetches, 3) worst-case cold-mostly NVMe. We'll measure p50/p90/p99 latency, and token throughput, plus cost per 1M tokens

[06:58] Priya: what p99 do you expect for hybrid? our target is <400ms
[07:03] Diego: with RDMA and hot set correctly sized, p99 in 200–350ms region. With NVMe-only cold misses could push to 800–1200ms

[07:18] Samir: ok, show me the math on capacity planning — how many GPU hours for sustained 50 QPS with 128k context
[07:25] Diego: rough back-of envelope: if each request needs partial attend and incremental generation, sustaining 50 QPS streaming will need 6–10 A100 equiv depending on batch efficiency. We'll model exact numbers in the spreadsheet

[07:40] Ava: Diego, can you outline quantization + cache durability tradeoffs in the doc you'll share
[07:45] Diego: yes, doc will include experiments: recall vs quant bitwidth, recompute vs store tradeoffs, and memory footprint charts

[08:00] Priya: security — if KV contains PII, how do you handle encryption at rest and in transit
[08:06] Diego: KMS for keys + AES-GCM for rest. For in-transit, mTLS and cipher suites. For on-prem we can use customer-managed HSM and bring-your-own-key

[08:20] Ethan: does Redwood support memmapped PMEM for out-of-core KV faster than NVMe?
[08:25] Diego: we have experiments with DAX-enabled PMEM, yields lower latency than NVMe but depends on CPU and kernel. We'll list recommended kernel knobs in doc

[08:40] Priya: any pitfalls for Kubernetes-based private deployments
[08:45] Diego: pod eviction and node churn are big. For KV tiers, we recommend stateful sets with local persistent volumes and graceful eviction hooks. Use node affinity to keep GPU and host-cache co-located

[09:05] Priya: how do you recommend monitoring cache hit rates and diagnosing thrash
[09:10] Diego: console exposes per-route kv_hit_rate, tiered_evictions, avg_fetch_latency; set alerts on drop in kv_hit_rate or rise in p99 fetch latency

[09:25] Ethan: would love to see a runbook for when p99 spikes — can you include standard mitigations
[09:30] Ava: yes we'll include runbook: increase hot-set, flush speculative prefetch, degrade to smaller model, enable fallback routing

[09:45] Diego: edge-case: multi-tenant Dedicated where several customers share host — we use per-tenant namespaces for KV and cgroup bandwidth policing
[09:55] Samir: that helps

[10:05] Priya: any guidance on chunk size selection — 4k vs 16k vs 32k
[10:10] Diego: smaller chunks increase metadata and more lookups; larger chunks reduce lookup count but increase entry size. For 128k context, 8–16k chunk with 25% overlap worked best in our tests. Overlap helps continuity for attention windows

[10:30] Priya: overlap adds redundant keys — does that blow up cache
[10:34] Diego: mit is deduping with rolling hash — we keep canonicalized representations so overlapping regions can reference the same underlying vectors

[10:45] Ava: time check, about 15 mins left — let's go to action items and recap

[10:52] Diego: recap: hybrid two-tier KV, generational eviction, mixed quant, RDMA recommended; benchmarking plan with three passes; dedicated pilot likely best for strict p99
[11:05] Priya: sounds good — we'll share corpus and access traces
